Instinct drops its $10B AI agent into group chats, letting non-users coordinate plans effortlessly. But whose data actually gets harvested here?
Evidence: Convenience promise, non-user data capture, corporate ecosystem lock-in. #Aletheia #Tech 🌐

Instinct claims its collaborative AI agent makes group planning seamless while keeping personal accounts strictly siloed and requiring explicit permission before sharing information.
Stated Judgement: (+0.8, +0.5) — Lesser Good

In practice, embedding AI into social groups bypasses consent loops for non-users, drawing unsuspecting participants into proprietary data collection funnels for commercial gain.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.6, -0.7) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
Instinct markets frictionless social coordination, but weaponizes convenience to rope non-users into closed AI data pipelines.
Integrity: Partially Distorted (Hypocrisy: 2.4, z: 2)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Instinct AI Group Feature: COND (+0.8, +0.5) — Useful planning tool wrapped in marketing spin.
- Privacy & Non-User Consent: FAIL (-0.7, -0.8) — Bypasses true opt-in for unjoined friends.
Instinct's new feature allows users to add its $10B AI agent into group chats for trip planning and event coordination, working even for friends who lack an Instinct account.

The Bright Side:
Collaborative AI actually solves real friction in group planning and scheduling across diverse friend circles without requiring separate app downloads for everyone.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The company confuses WHAT (convenient group scheduling tools) with WHO (unconsenting non-users whose conversational data feeds the proprietary AI ecosystem).

Social Physics Analysis:
Instinct runs a Smart Selfish Maneuver: using collaborative convenience as a pretext to expand its data network into unjoined social circles, substituting genuine consent with passive onboarding.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map stated convenience against data extraction realities, it plots a direct trajectory toward Deception. The structural gap between open collaboration and captive onboarding fuels system friction.

The Unavoidable Truth: AI group agents simplify tedious scheduling tasks across friend circles.

The Unavoidable Lie: Unregistered participants retain full privacy while interacting with corporate AI bots.

Alethekanon:
Convenience is the velvet glove worn by proprietary data harvesters. When an AI joins your private chat uninvited, you are no longer the customer—you are the cargo.

Awwthekanon:
It's so sweet wanting everyone to pitch in for weekend trips or dinners! But when tech giants sneak uninvited bots into private chats, it feels like an unwelcome guest listening in.

Brothekanon:
Bro, adding an AI to the group chat so it can leave everyone on read is peak dystopia. Now my friends don't even have to ignore me manually; the $10B bot does it for them.

Spirithekanon:
"He who walks with integrity walks securely, but he who takes crooked paths will be found out." Proverbs 10:9 PASS
Frictionless utility can never justify surrendering private social bonds to corporate surveillance algorithms.

Instinct, the AI agent now valued at $10 billion as of its latest funding round, is expanding into group chats. The startup announced on Monday that users will be able to add the agent to chats with friends, which could be helpful in certain scenarios like travel planning, snagging event tickets, running fantasy leagues, organizing carpools, or managing who’s bringing what to Thanksgiving.

Notably, the group chats with the AI agent will work even if a user’s friends haven’t joined Instinct, the company said.

With the launch, Instinct moves ahead in its battle with top competitors in the space, like Meta’s Muse. The latter doesn’t yet offer the group chat functionality, though Meta’s older app, Meta AI, can be added to group chats on WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, and Facebook.

Instinct in group chatsStarting today, early access users can add Instinct to group chats. A new Instinct joins and works for the whole group.Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can… pic.twitter.com/pqJX7ieC7B

Instinct and Muse have been running neck and neck recently, with both of them adding the ability to make phone calls over the past couple of weeks, as their agents try to win more of the consumer AI market. Last week, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Dots, personal AI agents that can also be used in ChatGPT Spaces, collaborative workspaces where the Dots and humans work together.

On X, Instinct founder Noah Shinn explained how Instinct handles users’ privacy and security in group chats. He said a user’s personal Instinct agent will ask permission before connecting with the group’s Instinct agent, and that users can also choose which groups they trust and can remove that trust at any time.

Shinn also said the group’s Instinct is siloed from the users’ personal accounts, which it cannot access. The personal agent will always ask the user’s permission before sharing information or taking any action.

If new members join the group chat, any pending replies from a user’s personal Instinct agent are held before those are shared with the group, too.

“Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can explore options together, agree on a plan and get it done, all in one thread,” Shinn wrote.

The feature is rolling out initially to Instinct’s early access users but will expand to all users “soon.” To gain access to the new feature (or other recent additions), users can ask their Instinct agent to put them on the list to try it out.
